title: Visiting and good manners
goal: Visit a Sundanese home without making anyone uncomfortable: from knocking on the door to saying goodbye, including the unwritten rules about refreshments.
bekal: the refreshment rules nobody states but everybody follows

dialogs.title: Paguneman — Visiting Bu Éha's home
dialogs.intro: Bu Éha has invited Rani to drop by. Rani arrives with a box of cakes, and the whole conversation is a lesson in manners.

lines.speaker: Bu Éha:
lines.text: Waalaikumsalam. Mangga, Néng Rani! Sumangga lebet.
lines.id: Waalaikumsalam. Hello, Rani! Do come in.
lines.literal: waalaikumsalam. please, Néng Rani! please enter.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Hapunten ngaganggu, Bu. Ieu aya sakedik oleh-oleh.
lines.id: Sorry to bother you, ma'am. I brought you a little something.
lines.literal: sorry disturb, Bu. this there-is a-little gift.

lines.speaker: Bu Éha:
lines.text: Aduh, teu kedah repot-repot atuh. Hatur nuhun pisan. Mangga linggih.
lines.id: Oh, you really shouldn't have. Thank you so much. Please, sit down.
lines.literal: oh, not must trouble-trouble [atuh]. thank you very. please sit.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.id: Thank you, ma'am. Your home is lovely.
lines.literal: thank you, Bu. house-the lovely very.

lines.speaker: Bu Éha:
lines.text: Ah, saayana waé. Badé ngaleueut naon? Téh atanapi kopi?
lines.id: Oh, it's nothing special. What would you like to drink? Tea or coffee?
lines.literal: ah, what-there-is just. will drink what? tea or coffee?

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Teu kedah repot, Bu. Cai hérang ogé cekap.
lines.id: Please don't go to any trouble, ma'am. Water is fine.
lines.literal: not must trouble, Bu. water clear also enough.

lines.speaker: Bu Éha:
lines.text: Ih, ulah kitu. Téh haneut waé nya, hawana tiris.
lines.id: Oh, don't be like that. Some hot tea, then, it's chilly.
lines.literal: oh, don't like-that. tea warm just [nya], air-the cold.

lines.speaker: Bu Éha:
lines.text: Sumangga diraosan koékna. Damel nyalira kamari.
lines.id: Do try the cakes. I made them myself yesterday.
lines.literal: please be-tasted cake-the. make self yesterday.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Raos pisan, Bu! Sanés ti toko geuning.
lines.id: They're delicious, ma'am! So they're not from a shop.
lines.literal: tasty very, Bu! not from shop it-turns-out.

lines.speaker: Bu Éha:
lines.text: Sok, seueurkeun. Ulah éra-éra di dieu mah.
lines.id: Go on, have more. Don't be shy here.
lines.literal: go-on, make-more. don't shy-shy at here [mah].

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Punten, Bu. Abdi badé amit mundur, tos wengi.
lines.id: Excuse me, ma'am. I'd better be going, it's late.
lines.literal: excuse-me, Bu. I will take-leave withdraw, already night.

lines.speaker: Bu Éha:
lines.text: Mangga, ati-ati di jalan. Sing sering ka dieu, nya.
lines.id: Of course, take care on the way. Come again soon.
lines.literal: please, careful at road. may often to here, [nya].

notes: **Sumangga** is the most polite form of *mangga* (please, go ahead). It's used with guests, elders and in speeches. Day to day, *mangga* is polite enough.
**Linggih** = to sit (lemes, for others), the respectful form of *diuk*/*calik*. Notice the host uses *linggih* for the guest, while the guest uses *calik* for themselves: *abdi calik di dieu*.
**Hapunten** = sorry (lemes); loma: **hampura**. Not the same as *punten*, which means excuse me. *Hapunten* is for real mistakes; *punten* is for opening a conversation.

**Saayana** = nothing special, "just what there is." *Ah, saayana waé* is the standard reply to any compliment on the host's home, cooking or belongings. Playing down your own things is a fixed part of Sundanese manners, and there's no need to argue.
**Diraosan** comes from *raos* (tasty, taste): "be tasted, try some." The loma form is *dirasaan*. It's the word a host uses when inviting a guest to try the food.
**Amit mundur** = to take your leave. It's the most polite way to say goodbye and very typically Sundanese. The short form is just *amit* or *punten, abdi badé amit*.

grammars.title: The unwritten rules of refreshments
body: This isn't grammar, but it decides how your visit goes more than any grammar point. Refreshments in Sundanese etiquette always follow the same order, and following it marks you at once as someone who knows how to behave.

head: Step
The host says
The guest replies
What's really going on
rows: the first refusal is **required**, and nobody takes it seriously
you must taste it, even just a little
you may stop once you've tasted it

after: ⚠️ Step 1 is the one newcomers break most often. Accepting the first offer straight away (*muhun, kopi*) isn't wrong, but it sounds hasty. Declining once, then accepting, is the expected rhythm.
⚠️ Step 3 matters too: refreshments left **completely untouched** make the host feel they've failed. One bite is enough, and there's no need to finish.

If you really can't eat or drink (fasting, allergy, illness), give the reason openly: *Hapunten Bu, abdi nuju puasa* or *Hapunten, abdi alérgi ka kacang*. A clear reason is happily accepted; it's refusing without one that makes things awkward.

sections.title: A visit from start to finish

head: Step
What you say
English
rows: Here's a little something for you.
Please don't go to any trouble, ma'am.
Excuse me, I'd better be going.
It's late, I'm afraid I'll oversleep tomorrow.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Taking your leave **always** needs a reason, even a simple one that everyone knows is a formality. Standing up and saying "I'm going home" with no reason feels abrupt. *Tos wengi* (it's late), *aya acara deui* (I have another appointment), *sieun kaburu hujan* (before the rain comes): all of them work.

blocks.title: What the host says
items: **Mangga, sumangga lebet.** — Please, do come in.
**Badé ngaleueut naon?** — What would you like to drink?
**Sing sering ka dieu.** — Come and visit often.

head: Basa Sunda
English
When to use it
rows: *Kersa lebet?* = would you kindly come in?

blocks.text: **Sumuhun** needs special care: it's the most respectful "yes," used with people much older or of high standing. In everyday conversation in Bandung, *muhun* is enough. You'll hear *sumuhun* more at religious gatherings, ceremonies and in front of elders.

blocks.title: Asking permission and saying no politely
items: **Punten, nyuhunkeun widi badé ka cai.** — Excuse me, may I use the bathroom?
**Punten, tiasa nyuhunkeun tulung?** — Excuse me, could you help me?
**Hapunten pisan, abdi teu tiasa.** — I'm so sorry, I can't.
**Hapunten, aya acara sanés.** — Sorry, I have something else on.
**Insya Allah, upami teu aya halangan.** — God willing, if nothing gets in the way.
**Engké abdi wartosan deui nya.** — I'll let you know later, okay?

blocks.text: The last two lines are the Sundanese way of saying no without saying no, and both are very common. If you get an answer like that, it often means "most likely not," and pushing further makes both sides uncomfortable. This side of the language isn't in any dictionary, but it shapes every social relationship.
